meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Talent is God-given; be humble. Fame is man-given; be thankful. Conceit is self-given; be careful'?
meta.ogDescription: A three-beat Wooden maxim. Credited to his 1972 memoir — but not confirmed against the book itself.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote lists this line under Wooden’s memoir They Call Me Coach (1972), written with Jack Tobin, and the wording there matches exactly. We stop short of calling it verified: Wikiquote gives no page and the Internet Archive’s scan is lending-restricted, so we could not read the book to confirm it.

source.excerpt: Talent is God-given; be humble. Fame is man-given; be thankful. Conceit is self-given; be careful.
trail: Wikiquote’s John Wooden page ↗ lists this line in its section for They Call Me Coach (1972), and the wording there is identical to the version in circulation.
Wikipedia’s bibliography ↗ confirms the book exists as described — They Call Me Coach, John Wooden with Jack Tobin, 1972, Word Books, with later revised editions.
The Internet Archive holds a 1972 scan ↗, but it is lending-restricted: neither its full text nor its search-inside index is publicly readable, so we could not confirm the page.
Quote Investigator ↗ has not investigated this saying, so there is no specialist finding that would override or refine Wikiquote’s attribution.
source.excerptNote: The wording above matches Wikiquote’s transcription character for character, which is worth something: it means the sentence has not drifted in the way most circulated maxims do.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of John Wooden and his publishers
source.rightsNote: They Call Me Coach was first published in 1972, long after the 1930 cutoff for United States public domain, so the text is in copyright. Rights sit with Wooden’s estate and the book’s publishers.

author.name: John Wooden
author.heading: About John Wooden
author.bio: John Robert Wooden won ten NCAA championships in twelve years at UCLA, including seven in a row, and was the first person inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame as both a player and a coach. He is remembered less for the trophies than for the teaching — short, plain maxims delivered to teenagers, and the “Pyramid of Success” he built around the idea that success is something you measure against yourself.

context.heading: Three gifts, three warnings
lead: The line is built like a coach’s chalk talk: three sources of status, three different responses. What you were born with is not yours to boast about; what the crowd gives you can be taken back; the only one you manufacture yourself is the one to watch.
Wooden coached teenagers who were about to become famous — Lew Alcindor and Bill Walton among them — which is the context that makes the third clause the point of the whole sentence.
context.pull: Conceit is the only one on the list you give yourself.
